splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability requires all actuarial assumptions to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running during the period of absconding.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authorization for such tolling, and the term expires as set in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1)—which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim—when bringing successive motions under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any previously presented claim on top of § 2255(h) requirements. If not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules such as mail-in ballot receipt deadlines. The resolution affects whether election administration challenges must wait until post-election disputes or can proceed before votes are cast.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging election rules that allegedly affect the counting of votes in their races.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive interest is insufficient to establish the concrete, particularized injury required for Article III standing to challenge ballot-counting rules pre-election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity—which requires ambiguities in criminal statutes to be resolved in the defendant's favor—trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails, creating a significant split affecting criminal sentencing nationwide.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations in the criminal sentencing context, requiring ambiguities to be resolved in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous sentencing guidelines or criminal provisions, deferring to the agency's anti-defendant reading.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text does not mention such offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is entitled to controlling deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This split directly affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so conspiracy convictions count as career-offender predicates.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so the commentary impermissibly expands the definition and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' in the safety valve provision means defendants must meet all three listed criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This governs whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and directly affects the liberty of criminal defendants.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive (all three required to disqualify)
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies)
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three listed criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), may be considered as an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in the law—particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 'stacked' § 924(c) sentences—as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others permit them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to authorize such consideration, but some circuits have held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in attempting to authorize such consideration.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release that is expressly intended to punish the defendant for the violation of supervised release conditions, rather than solely to address the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentencing at supervised release revocation. The Sixth Circuit, under United States v. Lewis, permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust inherent in the supervisory relationship.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Punishment is not the proper purpose
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentencing is to sanction the breach of trust in the supervisory relationship, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from the denial of a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (60 days for government parties) or the criminal deadline (14 days). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but a minority of circuits apply the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline of Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the shorter criminal appeal deadline of Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. Some circuits apply a categorical approach requiring a federal-law match, while others hold that any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of whether the substance is on federal schedules.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' includes state-law drug offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: State offense must match federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor, creating a split with significant practical consequences for debtors who convert in good faith.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity are property of the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with § 348(f)(1)(A)'s purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus or may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement that affect the execution of their sentences, or whether civil rights actions remain available. This split has persisted for over half a century and affects thousands of prisoner litigation cases annually, including First Step Act earned time credit disputes.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including earned time credits and transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought through habeas corpus and not civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights actions (Bivens or § 1983) to challenge conditions of confinement even when habeas relief might also be available, as long as they do not seek release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law—specifically the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 'stacked' sentences for § 924(c) gun offenses—as one factor among others when evaluating compassionate release motions under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts evaluating compassionate release motions may weigh non-retroactive statutory changes as a contributing factor. The Fourth Circuit permits such consideration while the Seventh and Eighth Circuits categorically prohibit it. SCOTUS has granted cert to resolve this question.

positions.label: May consider non-retroactive changes
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor among others in evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant compassionate release.

positions.label: May not consider non-retroactive changes
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under § 2255 — such as claims of legal error in the original conviction or sentence — may also be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. This affects thousands of prisoners seeking sentence reductions.

positions.label: Such factors may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in the original conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Such factors may not be considered
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the legality of the original conviction or sentence must be raised through habeas proceedings and cannot serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
